title: Accounts Merge
description:
Each entry of `accounts` is a list whose first element is a person's name and whose remaining elements are email addresses belonging to that account.

Two accounts belong to the same person if they share **at least one** email, even when the names differ in other accounts of the same person. (Two accounts with the same name but no common email may be different people.)

Merge the accounts. Each merged account should list the name first followed by its emails in **sorted** order. The merged accounts themselves may be returned in any order.

examples.explanation: The first two John accounts share johnsmith@mail.com and merge. The third John has no email in common and stays separate.
The first two accounts share nothing directly, but the third account bridges them, so all three collapse into one.

constraints: Names and emails are non-empty ASCII strings.
The first element is a name; the others are valid emails.
hints: Model it as connectivity: accounts that share an email are in the same component.
Union-find over account indices: map each email to the first account index that had it; when another account has the same email, union the two indices.
Afterwards, group emails by the root of their account and sort each group. Use the name from the root (any account in the group has the same person's name).
approach:
**Shared emails define connected components over account indices; union-find finds them in near-linear time.** Keep `owner[email]`, the first account index seen with that email. Scanning each account, an email already in `owner` means this account and the owner are the same person, so `union` them. After one pass every account's root identifies its person.

Then bucket emails by `find(owner[email])`, sort each bucket, and prepend the name of the root account. Any account in the component carries the same person's name, so the root's name is fine.

**Why union-find rather than DFS:** DFS over an email graph also works (build adjacency between the first email of an account and each other email, then traverse), but union-find needs no explicit graph and is shorter. With path compression and union by rank (or the path-halving shown), each operation is effectively O(1) amortised, so the sort dominates.

**Common mistakes:** unioning on names (wrong: different people may share a name), forgetting to sort emails, letting duplicate emails inside a single account create duplicates in the output (using a set per group avoids this), and recursive `find` without compression degrading to O(n).

**Interview follow-ups:** How would you do this with DFS and what is the memory cost? How does union by rank differ from path compression and why do you want both? If accounts arrive as a stream, how do you answer 'same person?' queries online? (Union-find handles that naturally.)

complexity.time: O(N * K log(N * K)) for N accounts with up to K emails (the sort dominates)
